topic: The Transformational View of Derivatives: The Local Scaling Factor
target_audience: First-year university students or advanced high school calculus students

sections.title: Introduction: The Number Line Stretcher
lecture_lines: Forget graphs for a moment.
Imagine a function as a mapping between number lines.
It morphs the input space into the output space.
Like a rubber band being pulled and compressed.
Points land on new positions after the transformation.
animations: Display two parallel horizontal lines representing Input x and Output y in #FFFFFF.
Label points on the x-line and show a point 'x' moving at a constant speed.
Draw a mapping arrow from 'x' on the input line to a point 'y' on the output line.
Visualize the mapping as a rubber band being pulled, showing non-uniform stretching.
Highlight the morphed segments of the output line in #FFFF00 to emphasize the transformation.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Linear Transformations
lecture_lines: Linear functions like y equals 3x scale space uniformly.
Every interval is stretched by a constant factor.
The slope is simply this constant stretching factor.
animations: Display the formula y = 3x and two number lines in #FFFFFF.
Show a small interval 'dx' on the input line mapping to a 3x larger interval 'dy' on the output line.
Move the 'dx' interval across the input line to demonstrate the scaling factor remains constant at 3.

sections.title: The Core Concept: Local Linearity
lecture_lines: For non-linear functions, stretching is not constant.
Some regions expand while others compress.
Zoom in infinitely on any specific point.
The transformation looks like a simple linear stretch.
This is the principle of local linearity.
animations: Display f(x) = x^2 mapping between number lines with non-uniform stretching.
Apply a heat map to the input line: #FF0000 for high stretch areas and #0000FF for compression.
Introduce a magnifying glass circling a specific point 'a' on the input line.
Zoom into point 'a' to show the transformation appearing as a simple, uniform linear stretch.
Highlight the locally linear segment in #90EE90 to confirm the concept of local linearity.

sections.title: Defining the Derivative as a Scaling Factor
lecture_lines: The derivative f prime of x is a ratio.
It represents the local scaling factor at a point.
Values greater than one indicate local expansion.
Values between zero and one indicate local compression.
Negative values mean the space is being flipped.
animations: Display the derivative formula f'(x) = dy/dx in #FFFFFF.
At x=3, show a tiny increment dx = 0.001 on the input line.
Show the resulting change dy = 0.006 on the output line, highlighting the 6x expansion.
Label the local scaling factor as '6' in #FFFF00 near the output line.
Show a mapping where f'(x) is negative, causing the output arrows to flip or cross.

sections.title: Character Application: The Speed-Changing Chameleon
lecture_lines: A chameleon walks steadily along the input line.
His shadow moves faster where the scaling factor is high.
The shadow crawls slowly in compressed regions.
animations: Show a chameleon [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/chameleon.png] walking at a constant speed along the input number line.
Where f'(x) is large, show the chameleon's [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/chameleon.png] shadow on the output line moving significantly faster.
Where f'(x) is small, show the shadow crawling slowly, representing local compression.

sections.title: Summary: The Derivative as a Local Map
lecture_lines: The derivative unifies slope and transformational views.
It tells how space is resized at every point.
Calculus is the study of local scaling.
animations: Show a complex grid [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/grid.svg] being distorted by a non-linear transformation.
Zoom in on a tiny portion of the grid [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/grid.svg] until the distortion looks like a uniform, linear scaling.
Highlight the final text 'Derivative = Local Scaling Factor' in #FFFFFF at the center of the screen.
